Series::LinearAlgAccessor::vdot¶

Back to Series::LinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::LinearAlgAccessor::vdot(const Series& other) const
Series SeriesLinearAlgProxy::vdot() const
Series Series::vdot(const Series& other) const

What It Does¶

vdot() computes the Hermitian inner product of two one-dimensional Series. It conjugates the left vector, multiplies corresponding positions, and sums:

vdot(x, y) = sum(conj(x[i]) * y[i], over i)

For real values, conjugation changes nothing, so vdot() and dot() produce the same number. For complex values, the distinction is essential: changing which operand is conjugated can change both the sign and magnitude of the imaginary component.

The Hermitian Inner Product¶

For complex vectors, vdot() is the inner product that behaves like a squared length when a vector is paired with itself. Every self-product is conj(z) * z = |z|^2, a nonnegative real value. Swapping different operands conjugates the scalar result:

vdot(y, x) = conj(vdot(x, y))

That symmetry is the practical reason operand order must remain visible in complex code.

Parameter¶

other (const Series&) The right vector. Both operands must be one-dimensional and have equal length. There is no broadcasting.

Returns¶

Series A rank-zero scalar. Its dtype follows the numeric operation; complex input produces a complex scalar.

Gradient¶

vdot() is built from conjugation, elementwise multiplication, and summation, so tracked inputs participate in reverse-mode propagation according to those operations’ complex-sensitivity rules.

For real vectors, the familiar result is identical to dot():

dL/dx = y
dL/dy = x

For complex calculations, keep the operand order deliberate because vdot(x, y) conjugates x, not y.

Examples¶

Example 1. Real vectors produce the ordinary inner product.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).linearalg.vdot(
    pluss::make_series({4.0, 5.0, 6.0})) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=32

Example 2. Complex input shows exactly what left conjugation changes.

using Complex = std::complex<double>;

auto left = pluss::make_series(
    std::vector<Complex>{{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, -1.0}}, {2});
auto right = pluss::make_series(
    std::vector<Complex>{{2.0, -1.0}, {4.0, 2.0}}, {2});

std::cout << "dot=" << left.linearalg.dot(right) << "\n";
std::cout << "vdot=" << left.linearalg.vdot(right) << "\n";

Without conjugation, the paired products sum to 18 + 5j. With left conjugation:

conj(1 + 2j)(2 - 1j) + conj(3 - 1j)(4 + 2j)
= (1 - 2j)(2 - 1j) + (3 + 1j)(4 + 2j)
= 10 + 5j

Output¶

dot=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=complex128, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=(18+5j)
vdot=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=complex128, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=(10+5j)

Example 3. Continuing with the complex vectors from Example 2, swapping operands conjugates the result.

std::cout << "forward=" << left.linearalg.vdot(right) << "\n";
std::cout << "reverse=" << right.linearalg.vdot(left) << "\n";

Output¶

forward=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=complex128, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=(10+5j)
reverse=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=complex128, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=(10-5j)

Example 4. Pair the same left vector from Example 2 with itself to obtain its squared complex length.

std::cout << left.linearalg.vdot(left) << "\n";

For left = [1+2j, 3-1j], the real scalar is |1+2j|^2 + |3-1j|^2 = 5 + 10 = 15.

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=complex128, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=(15+0j)

Example 5. Rank is part of the contract.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}}).linearalg.vdot(
      pluss::make_series({{3.0, 4.0}})) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << e.what() << "\n";
}

Output¶

vdot: expected two 1D Series

Example 6. Equal vector lengths are required.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::make_series({1.0}).linearalg.vdot(
      pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0})) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::cout << e.what() << "\n";
}

Output¶

vdot: inputs must have the same length

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • vdot(left, right) conjugates left only.

  • Both operands must be one-dimensional and equally long.

  • There is no shape broadcasting.

  • For real-only code, dot() may communicate intent more directly because conjugation has no effect.

Summary¶

vdot() is the strict complex-aware vector inner product. It returns sum(conj(left) * right) as a scalar and rejects non-vector inputs.
